name: Hearthway Furniture Rental
sector: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
location: Fictional operating unit in the Raleigh–Durham, North Carolina metropolitan area, United States.
operations: Hearthway Furniture Rental is a fictional analogue of CORT's residential furniture rental operation. Its modeled district serves households furnishing temporary homes, including relocating employees, students and military families. Customers select packages or individual pieces, agree rental terms and arrange delivery, setup and eventual pickup. Returned furniture passes through inspection, cleaning and, where appropriate, repair before another rental; assets retired from rental service pass to an associated outlet. This scope excludes workplace furnishings, events, apartment brokerage and destination services. The operating unit comprises one distribution warehouse with a refurbishment area, two rental showrooms and one associated outlet. Synthetic ordinary scale is 900 active household leases, 12,000 individually identified furniture pieces across customer homes and district locations, about 45 new rental orders and 40 completed lease returns per week, plus extensions, exchanges, repairs and outlet replenishment. Approximately 70 furniture pieces move into outlet stock each week. Four delivery crews and a separate warehouse and repair workforce perform physical work. The six modeled workers are recurring computer-use decision owners within that larger unit, not its entire staff. The district has five synthetic years of operating history, including multiple rental cycles, item-level repair histories, seasonal demand, customer preferences and outlet sell-through records. Routine work products include quotations, customer requirement records, availability reconciliations, asset allocations, repair instructions, dispatch manifests, retirement authorizations and outlet pricing recommendations.

evidence.text: Residential rental commitments, asset availability, repair readiness, dispatch capacity and outlet disposition form one interdependent operating cycle.
evidence.basis: Derived from the sourced service stages and role families in e1-e6 and e9-e10: commitments consume reusable furniture, returns create preparation work, and retirement removes assets from future rental supply. The responsibility choices in e7-e8, two teams and six decision owners model these dependencies; they are not a claim about CORT's reporting structure.

evidence.text: Hearthway is a mature Raleigh–Durham residential rental district with 900 active leases, 12,000 furniture pieces, two rental showrooms, one warehouse, one outlet and four delivery crews.
evidence.basis: Invented bounded-unit scale supports ordinary concurrent leases, returns, repair queues and outlet turnover. The weekly workload and five-year history in operations are scenario assumptions, not CORT counts.

evidence.text: The modeled unit uses explicit asset states, customer acceptance records, repair release evidence and delegated spending limits.
evidence.basis: Invented operating rules make decisions reproducible. Asset identity, physical location, condition and future reservation are separate fields. A planned pickup is not a receipt, a repair estimate is not release evidence, and retirement approval is not a completed sale.

evidence.text: The inspected catalog supports proposed analytical and service-record workspaces, but does not establish a functioning furniture rental lifecycle system.

These support customer requirements and cross-worker review records. Ticket closure does not execute a lease, reserve furniture or prove physical completion. Workers can build evidence-linked comparisons and instruction schedules from supplied snapshots. Formula coverage, concurrent editing, permissions and reset require validation. software.capability: Furniture rental lifecycle: lease item history, availability by date, readiness holds, reservations, actual returns and rental-to-outlet transitions
software.reference_product: Furniture rental management system; product unspecified
software.rationale: Essential behavior requires asset-level custody and condition independent of future reservations, prevention of conflicting commitments, release after documented preparation, and removal from rental supply before outlet sale. Inspected candidates did not establish this combination. Future execution must provide a validated domain environment or an explicit external system actor returning transaction acknowledgments. Generic tables must not be presented as an equivalent rental engine.

outlines.title: Allocate returned furniture between immediate reuse, repair and reserve
outlines.objective: Convert actual returns and preparation capacity into a defensible asset allocation that supports upcoming household commitments and leaves accurate readiness and reservation records.
outlines.decision_problem: Which returned pieces should receive scarce repair capacity, which ready pieces should be reserved, and which customer packages require an accepted alternative? Start with concurrent rental commitments, expected and actual returns, existing stock, repair histories and a constrained labor budget. w1 distinguishes mandatory household requirements from acceptable substitutions. w2 reconciles custody, condition and reservations and identifies which expected returns cannot yet support an allocation. w4 develops repair sequences with labor, materials and readiness dependencies. w3 tests whether resulting allocations can be staged and delivered within actual route and building constraints. w5 compares service consequences and incremental repair costs and authorizes a plan within budget. Workers issue customer-specific commitments, asset instructions and repair priorities. External technicians and crews then supply actual completion and movement reports; w2, w4 and w3 reconcile those reports, while w1 revises affected commitments and w5 resolves material tradeoffs. Completion requires supported final allocations or explicit unresolved shortages, not merely an approved spreadsheet.

outlines.title: Retire an aging furniture cohort and establish its outlet sale plan
outlines.objective: Choose which aging assets should remain available for rental and which should enter the outlet, then reconcile the financial and inventory consequences of the selected disposition.
outlines.decision_problem: When does an asset's expected additional rental contribution justify another repair and rental cycle instead of outlet sale, and how should approved outlet stock be priced and grouped? Use item histories, utilization, forward demand, repair estimates, outlet sale history and constrained floor space. w2 establishes the candidate population and excludes assets with active rental commitments or unresolved custody. w4 assesses the work and evidence needed for each rental or resale condition standard. w6 estimates achievable prices, time to sell and space consumption for individual pieces and compatible room groupings. w5 compares incremental rental contribution against repair cost, idle time and net resale proceeds, including uncertainty and minimum rental reserves. Retirement decisions become item-specific instructions that w2 reconciles with external transfer acknowledgments. w6 uses actual received condition and stock to finalize the permitted pricing plan and later interprets supplied sales results; w5 decides whether remaining pieces warrant a markdown, continued holding or another authorized disposition. No sale is inferred from a transfer or price approval.

outlines.title: Resolve lease extensions and staged pickups against future commitments
outlines.objective: Turn changing household departure needs into accepted lease and pickup instructions while preserving an accurate future supply picture.
outlines.decision_problem: Which combination of extension, staged pickup, exchange or revised future allocation can satisfy an existing household without silently consuming furniture already expected by another customer? Start with active lease item lists, customer requests, a fixed tariff, future reservations, eligible alternatives and route capacity. w1 interprets the supplied lease rules, calculates customer options and distinguishes requested changes from accepted amendments. w2 traces the requested retained pieces into future commitments and develops feasible asset alternatives without treating tentative pickups as receipts. w3 compares combined and separate visits using building access, truck volume and crew time. Their joint comparison determines which options w1 may present and which require a different commitment. Accepted responses control the lease-change and dispatch instructions. External system and crew acknowledgments then establish what actually changed and what was collected; w2 reconciles item custody and future availability, w3 closes or reschedules incomplete stops, and w1 prepares the exact billing handoff and customer confirmation. The cycle ends with consistent lease, pickup and future-allocation facts or an explicit unresolved exception.

assumptions: All Hearthway locations, scale, workloads, staffing levels, history and delegations are synthetic. The six worker identities describe selected recurring decision owners within a larger operating unit.

Source repair was conducted September 6, 2026. Accessible CORT blog articles replace inaccessible main-site service and pricing pages. Supplied successful captures ground inspection, outlet disposition, operations role families and customer groups. Unsupported job-posting duties are narrowed to captured role descriptions or labeled as inferences.
Real-company articles describe offerings at their publication dates. Their marketing language is not a service guarantee, current tariff, contractual entitlement or employee delegation.

The ordinary asset population extends well beyond any episode's affected items. Seeded history should include unaffected leases, stock, prior repairs, reservations and outlet transactions so local decisions have meaningful opportunity costs.

Two functional teams are an inferred organization. The inventory controller retains one identity and shared access across both teams. Other workers receive operational summaries and underlying evidence needed for their decisions.

Every outline includes at least three substantive computer-use contributors. Reviews must change feasible options, resource commitments, pricing or downstream records; participation is not satisfied by acknowledgment alone.

Rental-ready, awaiting inspection, repair hold, outlet-approved and sold are synthetic business states. Location, custody, condition and reservation remain separate attributes, with explicit transition rules.

Each episode supplies fixed tariffs, lease amendment rules, condition standards, repair limits, cost assumptions, customer responses, travel times and approval thresholds. No episode depends on live prices, real employee identities or changing website content.

Drivers, delivery assistants, receiving staff, inspectors and repair technicians are explicit external physical actors. Their reports provide observations and actual execution facts; modeled workers still reconcile evidence, calculate alternatives and make decisions.
Regional capital approval and accounting posting are external functions. Episodes requiring them must supply requests and responsive acknowledgments rather than assuming approval or posting.
The associated outlet is included only as the disposition channel for the same residential rental asset pool. Independent new-furniture purchasing and unrelated outlet business are outside scope.
Software entries are proposals, not evidence of CORT adoption. Catalog flags and schema examples do not prove deployed UI, permissions, seeding, reset or integration.

Until s4 is resolved, executable episodes must explicitly use an external rental-system actor with validated transaction acknowledgments. Spreadsheet instructions and service tickets cannot themselves establish reservations, executed leases, repair releases or completed outlet sales.
